title: David's Wars and Growing Kingdom
overview: David defeats the neighboring peoples around Israel, gathers their wealth, and sets up a working royal government in Jerusalem.

parts.label: Philistines and Moab beaten (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Metheg Ammah is an unclear name, perhaps meaning "the bridle of the mother city"; it was likely a key Philistine stronghold (a later retelling in 1 Chronicles says Gath). In Moab, David had captured soldiers lie in rows, measured them with a cord, and killed two out of every three lengths; the text gives no reason, and the Jewish tradition that it was revenge for harm to David's family is only a guess.

parts.label: Victory over the Arameans (vv. 3-8)
parts.note: Hadadezer ruled Zobah, a powerful kingdom in what is now Syria, and David also crushed the forces from Damascus who came to help him. David crippled most of the captured chariot horses by cutting their leg tendons so they could never be used in war again, and the numbers here differ somewhat from the parallel account in 1 Chronicles, probably through copying over the centuries.

parts.label: Gifts and dedicated treasure (vv. 9-12)
parts.note: Tou, king of Hamath, had been at war with Hadadezer, so he sent his son with rich gifts to congratulate David and win his friendship. David set apart the silver, gold and bronze for the LORD, and later tradition connects this treasure to the temple his son Solomon would build.

parts.label: Edom brought under control (vv. 13-14)
parts.note: The Hebrew here reads "Arameans," but many scholars think "Edomites" is meant, since the two words differ by one letter and verse 14 is about Edom; the Valley of Salt was probably near the south end of the Dead Sea. The repeated line that the LORD gave David victory wherever he went presents all this success as God's doing.

parts.label: David's royal officials (vv. 15-18)
parts.note: David is described as ruling with justice, and a list of officials follows: an army commander, a keeper of royal records, priests, a secretary, and Benaiah over the Kerethites and Pelethites, likely a foreign bodyguard with roots among the Philistines. The Hebrew says David's sons were "priests," which puzzles scholars because priests normally came from the tribe of Levi; 1 Chronicles calls them "chief officials" instead.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether these conquests credited to the LORD, including the killing of Moabite captives, should be read as actions God approved or as an honest record of ancient warfare that the Bible reports without endorsing.
think: When a leader's rule is praised as just but was built partly through brutal force, how do you weigh those two pictures against each other?
